parts.move: state the two-wave requirements for forming a stationary wave
parts.prompt: State the requirements on two progressive waves for them to form a stationary wave.
scheme: Equal frequency and wavelength, equal amplitude, and a fixed phase relationship
Travelling in opposite directions along the same line
Their superposition is stationary: ideal nodes have zero displacement and antinodes have maximum displacement
parts.answer: An ideal stationary wave is formed by two coherent waves of equal frequency, wavelength and amplitude travelling in opposite directions along the same line. Their interference fixes zero-displacement nodes and maximum-displacement antinodes instead of a travelling pattern.

parts.move: define node and antinode and state the characteristic spacings
parts.prompt: Define a node and an antinode of a stationary wave, and state the distance between adjacent nodes and between a node and its neighbouring antinode.
scheme: Node: zero displacement — waves arrive in antiphase
Antinode: maximum displacement — waves arrive in phase
Node to node: λ/2; node to adjacent antinode: λ/4
parts.answer: Nodes are points that never move (perfect destructive interference); antinodes swing hardest (constructive). The grid is fixed: neighbouring nodes half a wavelength apart, node-to-antinode a quarter.

parts.move: explain why a stationary wave transports no net energy along the medium
parts.prompt: Each of the two progressive waves carries energy. Explain why the stationary pattern they form transmits none.
scheme: Equal energy fluxes travel in opposite directions and cancel on average
Energy is trapped, sloshing between kinetic and potential within each loop
Antinodes and nodes only redistribute where the sloshing is visible
parts.answer: The pair send identical energy streams in opposite directions — their net flow is zero. Energy is confined, exchanging kinetic and elastic form inside each loop: the stationary wave is energy standing still in place, not vanishing.

parts.move: extract wavelength from measured node spacing in a standing microwave pattern
parts.prompt: A probe detects five successive minima spaced 3.0 cm apart along a microwave standing wave set up by reflection from a metal plate. Determine the wavelength and the frequency of the microwaves.
scheme: Node-to-node distance = λ/2 = 3.0 cm, so λ = 6.0 cm
parts.answer: Five minima mean 3.0 cm is half a wavelength: λ = 6.0 cm, and f = c/λ = 3×10⁸/0.060 = 5 GHz. Counting cold spots is a metre rule's way of weighing light.

parts.move: reject the idea that waves are destroyed at nodes
parts.prompt: A student says at a node the two waves 'cancel each other out of existence'. Explain what cancellation does and does not remove.
scheme: Only the displacement sums to zero — the waves' energy and identities survive
The waves pass through each other unchanged, as always in superposition
Evidence: past a node the antinode swings; remove one source and all energy returns to travelling
parts.answer: Nodes cancel displacement, never existence: the two waves glide through one another intact, continuing on. The proof is next door — the antinode's vigour shows the energy is still present, merely parked. Superposition subtracts motion at points; it does not subtract waves.

parts.move: correct loop-length-equals-wavelength confusion in stationary patterns
parts.prompt: A string vibrating in one loop (nodes at both ends) has length L. A student writes λ = L. Correct the claim and state the true relation for the fundamental.
scheme: One loop is half a wavelength: nodes are λ/2 apart
So λ = 2L for the fundamental
The full wave needs the loop plus its mirror half
parts.answer: A loop spans node to node — exactly half a wavelength — so the fundamental has λ = 2L, not L. The string holds half a wave; the other half is borrowed from the reflection.

parts.move: compute fundamental frequency from string length and wave speed
parts.prompt: A guitar string's fixed points are 0.64 m apart and waves travel along it at 320 m s⁻¹. Calculate the wavelength and frequency of its fundamental vibration.
scheme: Fundamental: λ = 2L = 2×0.64 = 1.28 m
parts.answer: The fundamental fits one loop between the bridges: λ = 2L = 1.28 m, so f = v/λ = 320/1.28 = 250 Hz — a middle C, roughly, of the string's own voice.

parts.move: compute resonant frequencies of a closed pipe by counting quarter-wavelength steps
parts.prompt: A pipe closed at one end is 0.40 m long. Calculate its fundamental frequency and its next allowed resonance. (speed of sound = 340 m s⁻¹)
scheme: Closed end node + open end antinode: L = λ/4 fundamental
Next allowed resonance is the third harmonic: L = 3λ/4 → f₃ = 3f₁ = 637.5 Hz
Even harmonics are impossible: no antinode–node pairing fits
parts.answer: A closed pipe must start at a node and end at an antinode: L = λ/4 gives f₁ = 212.5 Hz, and the next fit is three quarter-waves: f₃ = 3f₁ ≈ 638 Hz. Only odd harmonics answer — the pipe's geometry vetoes the even ones.

parts.move: transfer node-spacing reasoning to the uneven heating in a microwave oven
parts.prompt: A microwave oven (2.45 GHz) leaves cold bands in unmoved food. Calculate the spacing of the standing-wave nodes in the cavity and explain why a turntable is the fix.
scheme: Nodes every λ/2 ≈ 6 cm — the cavity walls set up a stationary pattern
Cold bands mark the nodes; rotating carries every part of the food through them and the antinodes
parts.answer: At 2.45 GHz λ ≈ 12 cm, so the reflected waves freeze into nodes every ~6 cm — precisely the cold spacing measured across an unmoved plate. The turntable is the standing-wave antidote: spin the food, and every bite samples both node and antinode.

parts.move: transfer standing-wave boundary conditions to a bridge's dangerous resonant mode shapes
parts.prompt: Marching soldiers break step across a bridge. Using the string analogy — fixed ends, allowed half-wavelengths — explain why one step rate can be far worse than others.
scheme: A span clamped at both ends admits only standing waves with L = nλ/2
Each mode has its own natural frequency f = nv/2L
Rhythmic steps matching a mode pump energy in; off-resonance steps largely miss
Breaking step removes the periodic shove that could lock onto a mode
parts.answer: A bridge, like a string, stores only half-wavelengths: L = nλ/2, each mode ringing at a fixed frequency. Marching feet deliver impulses at a chosen rate — and if that rate matches a mode, every step lands on the swing and energy piles up. Off step, the pushes stop phasing with the bridge and the danger passes.

parts.move: combine the superposition principle with wave functions to derive the stationary form and node spacing
parts.prompt: Two waves y₁ = A sin(ωt − kx) and y₂ = A sin(ωt + kx) travel in opposite directions. Their sum is y = 2A sin kx cos ωt (you may use this result). Explain from the form why nodes sit at x = 0, λ/2, λ, … and why no energy travels.
scheme: The shape factor sin kx is time-independent — the amplitude envelope stands still
Nodes where sin kx = 0: kx = nπ → x = nλ/2
Time part cos ωt makes every point oscillate together — a breathing shape, not a travelling one
Equal ±x fluxes in y₁, y₂ cancel: the net energy flow is zero
parts.answer: The sum factors into a fixed shape 2A sin kx and a common heartbeat cos ωt: positions of zero amplitude satisfy kx = nπ, i.e. x = nλ/2 — a standing grid. Since the envelope never moves, and the two travelling halves carried equal opposite fluxes, energy simply oscillates in place. The algebra holds the whole picture: nodes by geometry, stillness by factorisation.

parts.move: combine closed-pipe resonance with the wave equation to measure sound speed while cancelling the end correction
parts.prompt: A tube dipped in water resonates with a 512 Hz tuning fork at lengths 0.160 m and 0.490 m (first and second resonances). Write the λ–L relations including the end correction e, subtract them to remove e, and calculate the speed of sound.
scheme: Resonances: L₁ + e = λ/4 and L₂ + e = 3λ/4
Subtract: L₂ − L₁ = λ/2 = 0.330 m → λ = 0.660 m
The end correction cancels — a two-reading method needs no guess for e
parts.answer: Each resonance satisfies L + e = (odd)λ/4. The two equations differ by exactly λ/2, so 0.490 − 0.160 = 0.330 m is λ/2: λ = 0.660 m and v = 512×0.660 ≈ 338 m s⁻¹. Subtracting the resonance pair eliminates the mouth's end correction — two lengths, one honest speed.
